# The Night the Coolroom Died: A Cup Day Post, For You, Jonno

**Dear Jonno,**

You asked what happened. Twice. Then a third time with a sad face emoji, which is exactly the sort of thing you'd do. So here it is, the full unedited disaster, written down so you can read it on the train like the tragic novel it deserves to be.

Anyway.

**6.40am, Tuesday 3 November**

The compressor died sometime overnight. I know this because I woke up at 6.40 to a kitchen that felt wrong. Not silent-wrong. *Warm*-wrong. You walk into a walk-in that's been running all night and the air hits you like a bus. This air hit me like a bus.

Thermometer said 11 degrees. Eleven. That's not a fridge. That's a wine cellar for someone who's given up.

I stood in there for a good twenty seconds doing the maths. We had Cup Day lunch coming — 140 covers, fully booked, set menu, three courses. Service starts at noon. It's 6.40am. I am a sous-chef. Not a manager. Not a magician.

Then I rang Wally at Coldline. Wally, my beloved fridge man, the only person in Victoria who understands what a "Satra" is. He was nice about it, which somehow made it worse. He couldn't get to us till Wednesday. The part he needed was coming from Sydney. Sydney! On Cup Day. Sydney doesn't even know what a meat pie is, let alone care about our dairy.

**The Plan (such as it was)**

So here's what we did, and I want you to appreciate this because you would not have.

Everything went into two undercounters. Everything. The bar fridge. And Marta, who runs the café next door, opened up half her walk-in to us. Half. Not all of it. Half, because she's a businesswoman, and I respect that, and I also hate it.

We lost about $1800 of stock. Mostly dairy. Cream, milk, butter, yoghurt, a truly obscene amount of cheese. And the duck legs.

The duck legs were the worst. I want you to know that I grieved the duck legs. Not a bit. Properly. Six kilos of them, and they had to go in the bin, and I stood there with the bin lid open like it was a funeral. If you want to make fun of me, make fun of me for the duck legs. I don't care. The duck legs were worth it.

**Raff was off that day** so it was me running the pass, which means every single decision that went wrong and every single decision that went right was mine. I want that on the record.

**6.55am: The Beef Shin Incident**

The beef shin was still coming. Thirty kilos of shin, sitting in the walk-in that was now at 11 degrees and rising. The delivery driver wasn't going to come back. So me and Benny — Benny, my mate Benny, who is 5'7" and has the upper body of a meerkat — we took the thing down the laneway on a milk crate trolley. In the rain.

Thirty kilos. Milks. In the rain. Down a laneway that is cobbled, by the way, because this restaurant was built in 1883 and nobody has paved it since because why would you.

And then the wheel fell off.

Not "came loose". Fell off. Rolled off. Gone down the laneway. And Benny went after it, in the rain, in his chef shoes, and I stood there holding thirty kilos of beef shin with both arms like a bloody human wheelbarrow, and I could not move, and the trolley could not move, and the rain was doing that thing where it gets into your eyes and your ears and down the back of your neck.

There is no short version of this story. There is only the long version, which ends with us dragging a milk crate down a cobbled laneway with a missing wheel and a bin bag of beef shin swinging from one of the corners.

That's the whole morning. That happened before lunch.

**9.30am: Kev and the Esky**

We needed ice. Not ice for drinks. Ice for *product*. Temperature control. Which means buying ice, at 9.30am on Cup Day, from a servo.

Kev — Kev, who is 61 and has worked in kitchens since before I was born and who I would take a bullet for — filled the old esky from the servo. Fourteen bags. He counted them out loud. He counted them out loud and the servo bloke watched him and then asked, "You guys having a party or what?"

Kev looked him dead in the eye and said, "We open at twelve."

The servo bloke did not laugh. I think he was genuinely concerned for us. Which, fair.

Fourteen bags of ice went into one esky, and that esky became the most important object in the building. We still had to make dairy. We still had to make dessert. We still had to have a fridge that was technically a fridge and not just a cold room with ambition.

**12.15pm: We 86'd the Panna Cotta**

This is where it gets good, and by good I mean catastrophic but in a way that turned out fine.

Panna cotta was dead. No cream, no milk, no chance. So at 12.15pm I walked out to the floor and I 86'd it. Which in bistro language means we don't have it, and if you don't have it you find out about it at the table, in front of the guests, like a person with confidence.

So the dessert became affogato with whatever.

*Whatever* being the operative word. Affogato with whatever espresso we had, with whatever ice cream-ish thing we could salvage, with whatever had survived the walk-in. And here's the thing, Jonno, and I need you to sit down for this.

People loved it more.

Not just "it was fine". People actively, visibly preferred it. There was a table of six who asked what the panna cotta was going to be, because they'd heard about it from a friend, and when I said we'd run out, one of them actually said "oh good, this is better." Out loud. In front of me. While I was holding a tray.

The dessert that existed because of the disaster was better than the dessert we'd planned. I have thought about this every day since and I still don't have a theory. I think it might just be that when you've had a morning like ours, everything tastes like a win.

**Table 9**

A lady at table 9 — very nice lady, lovely, tipper, I'm not complaining about table 9 — looked out the window. Looked straight at me and Benny. At the milk crate. At the bin bag of beef. At the trolley with one wheel. At Kev and fourteen bags of ice.

And she asked if the beef was free range from the laneway.

I said, "It is now, ma'am."

She said, "Lovely."

**The Bill with Marta**

Marta let us have half her walk-in and she was very gracious about it, and then she told me the price of the favour, which was that I'd work it off in staff meal croissants. Which means I now owe her roughly three weeks of staff meals.

Three weeks of croissants. I ate a croissant on Monday and it felt like a loan repayment. I ate a croissant on Tuesday and it felt like a down payment. Jonno, I have never in my life been so aware of the weight of pastry.

**The Service**

And then lunch happened.

140 covers. Three courses. Set menu. Ran by me, because Raff was off. On a compressor that had died in the night, in a walk-in that hit 11 degrees, with half a café's walk-in and fourteen bags of servo ice holding the entire dairy program of a bistro together.

And it was the best service we did all year. I'm not being dramatic for the blog. I'm not making it a sob story. I'm just telling you what happened. Everyone was locked in. The whole room knew something was up — you can always tell, the way the room gets quieter and the team gets tighter — and nobody complained. Not one person sent food back. Nobody asked about the panna cotta except in a good way. The runner, the dishys, Kev, Benny, me, we all just... did it.

I did the pass alone for three hours and I don't remember a single moment of it being a problem. That's never happened to me before. That's not supposed to happen to me before.

If you'd been here you'd have lost your mind. You absolutely would. You'd have been in the middle of that laneway, in the rain, holding a milk crate, and at some point around 11am you'd have sat down on an upturned bucket and gone completely silent and then you'd have said something like "this is actually amazing" and made everyone emotional. That's what you did in 2019 when we did 200 covers with one down. You cried at a fried chicken plate. You have never had a hard day of work in your life that you didn't cry at a slightly nice thing.

**The Horse**

In the sweep I had a horse in called Ice Cold Lad. He came second last.

Second. Last.

The universe is taking the piss. The universe watched our coolroom die and then said, "and here's a horse for you, mate." That's on the record. He's alright, Ice Cold Lad. He's had a season. He's not the problem.

**A Few Other Things, Jonno**

- You moved to London in February and you've gone soft. Not "living in London" soft. *Soft* soft. You sent me a photo of a flat with a plant in it, Jonno. A plant. You water it. You told me you water it. You used to eat a cold meat pie out of the packet in the walk-in at 1am and now you're growing things and drinking wine that has a grape variety on the label. London has done something to you and I don't think it can be undone.
- You said you'd "come back for Cup Day" in 2027 and I believe you about as much as I believe Wally's ETA.
- I miss having you on the grill, which is a stupid sentence, and which is true.

**One More Thing**

Phil's response to all of this — and I'm including this because you'll like it — was to stand in the kitchen at about 7pm, look at the wreckage, and say:

"Just make it work, mate."

Which is not a plan. That is not a plan, Jonno. That is a vibe. If you write "just make it work" on the whiteboard and then the walk-in stays at 14 degrees on Saturday, nobody's coming. Wally's coming Wednesday and that's it.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. That's the whole business model. That's the entire industry. Every good kitchen in this country is one broken compressor away from a very interesting morning.

Anyway. That's what happened. That's the story.

I hope your plant's doing well.

**Come home ya flog.**

---

*(P.S. Mum says hi. She says you're too thin. She says bring back a hat.)*
